# John: "this is the work of God, that you believe"


The day after the feeding of the five thousand, the crowd finds Jesus across
the lake and asks him a question about works:

> "What must we do, to be doing the works of God?" Jesus answered them, "This
> is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent" (John
> 6:28–29).

The question is about works, and the answer is believing. This is the fourth
strand of sola fide, and John says the same thing elsewhere. Whoever believes in
the Son has eternal life and does not come into judgement (3:16–18, 3:36, 5:24),
and the Gospel gives this as its own purpose: "that by believing you may have
life in his name" (20:31).

## What both sides grant, and where they part

Nobody in this dispute denies the verse. They differ on what its believing is.

- **Calvin** reads it as trust. Christ calls faith a work only loosely: faith
  "brings nothing to God, but, on the contrary, places man before God as empty
  and poor, that he may be filled with Christ". It is "a passive work, to which
  no reward can be paid".
- **Aquinas** reads it as faith formed by charity, that is, faith made alive by
  love. He takes Paul to distinguish faith "only from external works", so that
  believing is itself an inward work. To believe *in* him, as the goal one
  moves toward, "is proper to faith
  living through the love of charity", and such faith "is the principle of all
  our good works" (*Super Ioannem* 6, lect. 3, n. 901). The Council of Trent
  describes justifying faith the same way: without hope and charity, faith
  "neither unites man perfectly with Christ, nor makes him a living member of
  His body" (Session VI, ch. 7).

So this strand has the shape of the other three: texts everyone accepts, and
one reading on which the conclusion turns. On Calvin's reading John supplies
faith alone without the readings the other strands depend on
(`johannine_strand_establishes`).
On Aquinas's it does not (`johannine_strand_rests_on_believing_as_trust`).

## John has no word for "justify"

Paul's verb for "justify" (δικαιόω) does not occur in John's Gospel. So the
strand has to step from "eternal life through believing" to "justified by faith
alone", and that step is an inference, not the meaning of a word. It is cited to
Calvin, whose comment on 6:29 speaks of the righteousness faith receives from
Christ. It is rated `plausible`. No cited source accepts the strand's premises
and rejects the step, but no cited source argues the step at length either.

## Luther's answer to Aquinas

Luther, in his own lectures on Galatians, answers the reading Aquinas gives of
John 6:29. He names "the scholastics", not Aquinas; the faith formed by charity
that he attacks is the reading Aquinas gives. On 3:11:
"The scholastics misconstrue this passage by saying: 'The just shall live by
faith, if it is a working faith, or a faith formed and performed by charitable
works.' … To speak of formed or unformed faith, a sort of double faith, is
contrary to the Scriptures." On 3:12: "Does not the Law command charity? … If
the law requires charity, charity is part of the Law and not of faith."

His argument runs: love is what the law commands, and "the law is not of faith"
(Galatians 3:12), so a faith that justifies because love forms it would justify
by the law after all.

The argument is encoded as a line of its own (`lutherLine`). Its two starting
points are ones Aquinas accepts: the text of Galatians 3:11–12, and that love of
God and neighbour is what the law commands (Deuteronomy 6:5). The step from them
is Luther's. Grant the step, and Aquinas's reading of John 6:29 falls
(`luther_answers_aquinas_from_galatians`). Without the step the texts do not
exclude his reading (`luther_answer_rests_on_his_step`). The step is rated
`disputed`, because Aquinas accepts both starting points and rejects the
conclusion. His reason for rejecting it is not yet cited here.

Two limits. Removing Aquinas's reading does not establish Calvin's: "not formed
by charity" is a weaker claim than "trust". And the Catholic reply rests on
Galatians 5:6, "faith working through love", which Trent cites (Session VI,
ch. 7). How Luther and Calvin read that verse is not yet encoded.

Calvin makes a neighbouring argument in the *Institutes* (III.xi.19), against
those who "pretend that the works excluded are ceremonial, not moral works". He
cites Galatians 3:10 and 3:12 and concludes that "the whole Law is spoken of
when the power of justifying is denied to it". That answers those who say Paul
excludes only ceremonial works. Aquinas does not say that. He says believing is
an inward work, formed by love. So Luther's argument, and not Calvin's, is the
one that addresses him.

## Where the strand stands in the whole dispute

The strand is one of the four strands of the Reformed case, and John's case,
Aquinas's and Luther's are parties to the sola fide dispute. Three things are
checked.

- **John supplies "through faith" without the other three strands.** Leave out
  the disputed readings in Paul, Luke and Acts. Keep what every strand shares:
  the verses on grace and works, and the answer to James. Sola fide still
  follows, with John 6:28–29 as the only route to faith
  (`johannine_strand_survives_the_other_three`).
- **John's disputed reading is not one the whole case depends on.** Grant
  Aquinas his reading of 6:29, keep the other three strands, and sola fide still
  follows (`believing_as_trust_not_load_bearing`).
- **John's case is not forced, and neither is any rival.** John's case and
  Aquinas's each defeat the other, that is, each contradicts the other and
  neither is better supported. So do Aquinas's and Luther's, John's and Trent's,
  and John's and the apocalyptic reading's. Each pair is a tie, because each
  side rests on a premise rated `disputed`.

## John 3:36: "whoever does not obey the Son"

Three chapters on, John sets two words side by side that a reader of this
debate cannot pass over:

> "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son
> shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36).

The verse sets *not obeying* against *believing*. Does believing, in John,
include obeying? And if it does, can faith alone be what saves? The record
points two ways, one on the word and one on the doctrine.

The Greek for "does not obey" (ὁ ἀπειθῶν) is read by the
commentators cited here as unbelief seen in what it does. Westcott: "believeth
not] disobeyeth. Disbelief is regarded in its activity." Calvin's comment takes
the clause of "all who do not believe in Christ". Among modern commentators,
Ridderbos: "'Disobeys' serves as a description of 'unbelief'". Carson takes the
verb as "disobeys", and adds that "failure to trust him is as much disobedience
as unbelief". No source has been found that argues from this word that believing
includes obeying.

The doctrine is another matter. Chrysostom, preaching on this verse, does deny that
believing is enough: "'Is it then enough,' saith one, 'to believe on the Son,
that one may have eternal life?' By no means." He does not argue from the word.
He argues from Jesus' saying in Matthew 7:21, "Not everyone who says to me,
'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven", and concludes: "though a man
believe rightly on the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, yet if he lead not a
right life, his faith will avail nothing towards his salvation" (*Homilies on
John* 31).

Chrysostom's argument is written out as starting points, a step and a conclusion
(`chrysostomLine`). Its starting points are two texts every reader here accepts.
The step from them to "faith does not suffice" is his. Three things are checked.

- Granted his step, his conclusion follows
  (`chrysostom_reads_john3_36_against_faith_alone`).
- The wording of the two texts does not settle it. One consistent reading holds
  both texts and that faith suffices; another holds both and that it does not
  (`john3_36_leaves_faiths_sufficiency_open`).
- His conclusion, written out as "faith does not suffice", and John's strand
  cannot both be held (`chrysostom_cannot_be_held_with_johns_case`). Whether the
  faith he means is the faith the Reformers mean is a further question, noted at
  that result.

The step is rated `disputed`. Calvin accepts both texts and denies the
conclusion: he reads the doing of Matthew 7:21 as including faith, and good
works as what follows faith. Among modern readers Chrysostom has company:
Stanley holds that "Endurance is a condition for final salvation", and reads
Matthew 7:21 so.

Chrysostom's case is heard in the main sola fide debate,
and so is the Reformed answer to it (below). His conclusion is general, so there
he meets every case that concludes that faith suffices: Paul's, Luke's, Peter's
and John's, and the Reformed answer. Each of those meets him in return, and
every one of the ties is between positions rated `disputed`. He does not meet
the arguments about Paul's word or Paul's gospel, and he contradicts no verse of
Paul's (`chrysostom_grants_the_pauline_texts`).

The standard lexicon (BDAG) on the word has not been read, and neither have the
commentaries of Brown, Schnackenburg and Barrett.

## The Reformed answer: obedience is sanctification

The Reformed do not deny what Chrysostom's texts say. Whoever does not obey the
Son shall not see life (John 3:36), and only the one who does the will of the
Father enters the kingdom (Matthew 7:21). They deny what he concludes from them.

On their reading the obedience these texts require is sanctification: the life
of good works, inward and outward, that follows faith as its fruit and its
evidence. It is necessary, for a faith that bears no such fruit is dead. But it
is not the ground of justification, and it is not a second thing added to faith
as its means. Modern Reformed and evangelical scholars put each part of this.

- On John 3:36, Ridderbos: "'Disobeys' serves as a description of 'unbelief'".
  Carson: "failure to trust him is as much disobedience as unbelief".
- On Matthew 7:21, Morris: "This is not salvation by works: the contrast is not
  between merit and grace, but between profession and way of life."
- On the place of works, Schreiner: "the works necessary for justification
  aren't the basis for salvation and in that sense don't contribute to
  salvation. They are the necessary evidence for and fruit of salvation." And:
  "the necessity of good works doesn't contradict sola fide" (p. 55). Hoekema:
  good works "must not be thought of as meritorious ... Yet they are necessary".
  Murray: "It is living faith that justifies".

Westminster says the same: good works "are the fruits and evidences of a true
and lively faith" (XVI.2), and the sanctification of the justified is distinct
from their justification (XIII.1, XI.1). So, read whole, John 3:36 says what its
first half says in terms: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life."

The reading is written out as a line of its own (`sanctificationLine`), and heard
in the main debate as the Reformed answer to Chrysostom. It is rated `disputed`.
Chrysostom accepts both texts and reads them the other way, and so does a modern
reader: Stanley holds that "Endurance is a condition for final salvation", and
reads Matthew 7:21 as making doing the Father's will a condition and not only its
evidence. The commentaries above were read through their e-book editions, so
they are cited by verse and not by page.

### Results

<a id="johannine_strand_establishes"></a>
**`johannine_strand_establishes`**

**John's strand, argued alone, delivers sola fide.** Grant that the
believing of 6:29 is trust, and the work God requires is believing, which earns
nothing. Sola fide then follows without the readings Paul's, Luke's and Peter's
strands depend on.

It does not show that John 6:29 is the only text used. Grace and "not
by works" come from the verses every strand shares and from the answer to
James.

```lean
theorem johannine_strand_establishes : Establishes johannineCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="thomistReading"></a>
**`thomistReading`**

Aquinas's reading, written out. Every text holds. The believing of 6:29 is faith
made alive by love, so it is not bare trust; justification is not by faith
alone; and faith without charity does not suffice. Grace and "not by works"
still hold: Aquinas excludes outward works, and grants that faith is God's gift.

```lean
def thomistReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.johannineBelievingIsTrust => False
    | Claim.justificationByFaithAlone => False
    | Claim.faithIsSufficient => False
    | Claim.salvationThroughFaith => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="johannine_strand_rests_on_believing_as_trust"></a>
**`johannine_strand_rests_on_believing_as_trust`**

**John's strand depends on reading believing as trust.** Grant Aquinas every
text the strand reads, and read their believing as he does, faith made alive by
love, and sola fide no longer follows.

So John's Gospel, like Paul's Galatians and Luke 7:50, reaches the conclusion
only through a reading: here, of what it is to believe *in* him.

```lean
theorem johannine_strand_rests_on_believing_as_trust : ¬Establishes
    thomistOnJohn
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="believing_as_trust_not_load_bearing"></a>
**`believing_as_trust_not_load_bearing`**

**The reading of believing as trust is not one the whole case depends on.**
Grant Aquinas that the believing of John 6:29 is faith formed by charity, keep
Paul, Luke and Acts as the Reformed read them, and sola fide still follows.

Losing the argument over John 6:29 costs the Reformed case one
strand and not its conclusion. It does not show that Aquinas would accept
the rest. He would not, and the package is not his position; it is the Reformed
case with one concession made.

```lean
theorem believing_as_trust_not_load_bearing : Establishes
    reformedGrantingAquinasOnJohn
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

**`concedingJohnReading`**

The Reformed reading with one concession: the believing of John 6:29 is not bare
trust, and everything else holds.

```lean
def concedingJohnReading : Valuation Claim :=

    match a with
    | Claim.johannineBelievingIsTrust => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="reformedGrantingAquinasOnJohn_is_satisfiable"></a>

That package can be held without contradiction, so
`believing_as_trust_not_load_bearing` is not true merely because its premises
could never all hold.

```lean
theorem reformedGrantingAquinasOnJohn_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    reformedGrantingAquinasOnJohn.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="johannineCase_is_satisfiable"></a>

### Luther's answer

<a id="lutherOnGalatiansThree"></a>
**`lutherOnGalatiansThree`**

Luther's step, on Galatians 3:11–12: the law commands love, and the law is not
of faith, so faith formed by charity would justify by the law. Rated `disputed`:
Aquinas accepts both starting points, the text and that the law commands love,
and denies the conclusion, holding that the faith which justifies is formed by
charity.

```lean
def lutherOnGalatiansThree : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work lutherGalatians
        (Bib.Locus.adLoc { book := Book.galatians, chapter := 3, verse := 12 }),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work lutherGalatians
          (Bib.Locus.adLoc
            { book := Book.galatians, chapter := 3, verse := 11 })],
    tradition := Tradition.reformedProtestant,
    confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

faith formed by charity, since love is what the law commands and the law is not

<a id="luther_answers_aquinas_from_galatians"></a>
**`luther_answers_aquinas_from_galatians`**

**Luther answers Aquinas from Galatians 3.** Grant what Aquinas grants,
Galatians 3:11–12 and that the law commands love, and grant Luther's step. Then
the believing of John 6:29 is not faith formed by charity: a faith that
justified because love formed it would justify by the law, and the law is not of
faith.

It does not show that Calvin's reading is thereby established. It
removes Aquinas's reading, and only if the step is granted.

```lean
theorem luther_answers_aquinas_from_galatians : Establishes lutherOnGalatians
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="luther_answer_rests_on_his_step"></a>
**`luther_answer_rests_on_his_step`**

**Luther's answer depends on his step.** The texts alone do not exclude
Aquinas's reading. On Aquinas's reading Galatians 3:11–12 holds, the law
commands love, and the believing of 6:29 is faith formed by charity. What
decides it is whether faith formed by charity counts as justification "by the
law". That is Luther's step, and Aquinas denies it.

```lean
theorem luther_answer_rests_on_his_step : ¬Establishes galatiansTextsAlone
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="lutherReading"></a>
**`lutherReading`**

The Reformed reading, on which the believing of John 6:29 is not faith formed by
charity, and everything else holds.

```lean
def lutherReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.johannineBelievingIsFormedByCharity => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="lutherOnGalatians_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`lutherOnGalatians_is_satisfiable`**

Luther's position can be held without contradiction, so
`luther_answers_aquinas_from_galatians` is not true merely because its premises
could never all hold.

```lean
theorem lutherOnGalatians_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    lutherOnGalatians.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="whyLutherAnswersAquinas"></a>
**`whyLutherAnswersAquinas`**

**Why Luther's answer stands against Aquinas.** Everything turns on Luther's
step: from Galatians 3:11–12 and the law's command of love, the believing that
justifies is not faith formed by charity. With the two texts accepted, Aquinas's
reading of John 6:29 cannot keep its one distinctive premise, that the believing
is formed by charity.

Unlike the Reformed distinction against Trent, this step is part of Luther's own
case: without it, the texts do not deliver his conclusion. So the answer is
exactly as strong as the step, which is rated `disputed`. The step is Luther's,
and the texts are accepted by both sides.

**Why *Luther on Galatians 3:11–12 (against faith formed by charity)* stands against *Aquinas on John 6:29 (faith formed by charity)*.**

- **The crux:** \\((P_{42} \land P_{43}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{41}\\), a premise of *Luther on Galatians 3:11–12 (against faith formed by charity)*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Granted:** \\(P_{42}\\), \\(P_{43}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(P_{41}\\) cannot be held together with \\((P_{42} \land P_{43}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{41}\\) and \\(P_{42}\\), \\(P_{43}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(P_{42}\\) Galatians 3:11–12 — none is justified by the law; the law is not of faith — *consensus*: Gal 3:11-12; [`luther-commentary-galatians-1998`](../../bibliography.md#luther-commentary-galatians-1998), ad loc. Gal 3:11
  - \\(P_{43}\\) Love of God and neighbour is what the law commands — *consensus*: Deut 6:5; Matt 22:37-40; [`luther-commentary-galatians-1998`](../../bibliography.md#luther-commentary-galatians-1998), ad loc. Gal 3:12
  - the step itself — *disputed*: [`luther-commentary-galatians-1998`](../../bibliography.md#luther-commentary-galatians-1998), ad loc. Gal 3:12; [`luther-commentary-galatians-1998`](../../bibliography.md#luther-commentary-galatians-1998), ad loc. Gal 3:11

<a id="chrysostomOnJohnThreeThirtySix"></a>
**`chrysostomOnJohnThreeThirtySix`**

Chrysostom's step, in Homily 31 on John: from John 3:36 and Matthew 7:21 to
"faith alone is not sufficient to salvation". Stanley, a modern reader, holds
works "a condition to final salvation" in the Synoptic Gospels, Matthew 7:21
among the texts. Rated `disputed`: Calvin accepts both texts and denies the
conclusion, and so do the modern Reformed readers cited for the answer.

```lean
def chrysostomOnJohnThreeThirtySix : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work chrysostomHomiliesJohn
        (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Homily 31, §1"),
    supporting := [Reference.work stanleyDidJesusTeach],
    tradition := Tradition.easternOrthodox, confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="chrysostomLine"></a>
**`chrysostomLine`** — Chrysostom on John 3:36 (believing is not enough without a right life)

**Chrysostom's line.** From "whoever does not obey the Son shall not see
life" (John 3:36) and "not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord'" (Matthew
7:21) to the conclusion that believing does not suffice without a right life.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{38} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{62} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; (P_{38} \land P_{62}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{26} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; \lnot P_{26}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

<a id="chrysostomOnJohn"></a>
**`chrysostomOnJohn`** — Chrysostom on John 3:36 (believing is not enough without a right life)

Chrysostom's argument as a position: the two texts, with his step.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{38} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{62} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; (P_{38} \land P_{62}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{26} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; \lnot P_{26}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="chrysostom_reads_john3_36_against_faith_alone"></a>
**`chrysostom_reads_john3_36_against_faith_alone`**

**Granted his step, Chrysostom's conclusion follows.** From John 3:36 and
Matthew 7:21, read as he reads them, believing does not suffice for salvation
without a right life.

His argument is valid, and its premises are two texts nobody
here disputes. It does not show that the step is sound. Calvin accepts
both texts and denies it, so the step is rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem chrysostom_reads_john3_36_against_faith_alone : Establishes
    chrysostomOnJohn
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="chrysostomOnJohn_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`chrysostomOnJohn_is_satisfiable`**

Chrysostom's position can be held without contradiction, on Aquinas's reading,
where every text holds and faith without charity does not suffice. So
`chrysostom_reads_john3_36_against_faith_alone` is not true merely because its
premises could never all hold.

```lean
theorem chrysostomOnJohn_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    chrysostomOnJohn.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="john3_36_leaves_faiths_sufficiency_open"></a>
**`john3_36_leaves_faiths_sufficiency_open`**

**The wording of John 3:36 and Matthew 7:21 leaves open whether faith
suffices.** One consistent reading holds both texts and that faith suffices: the
Reformed one, on which not obeying the Son is refusing to believe him. Another
holds both texts and that faith does not suffice: Chrysostom's and Aquinas's.

Neither side can settle the question by pointing at the
words. It does not show that the two readings are equally good. That is
a matter for the sources, and the page reports what they say.

```lean
theorem john3_36_leaves_faiths_sufficiency_open : Independent [p
    Claim.john3_36WhoeverDoesNotObey, p Claim.matthew7_21_23DoingTheWill] (p
    Claim.faithIsSufficient)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="johnWithChrysostom"></a>
**`johnWithChrysostom`**

John's strand and Chrysostom's argument, held together: every premise of
each.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{36} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{37} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; P_{40} \\
\text{(4)} \quad &amp; P_{1} \\
\text{(5)} \quad &amp; P_{2} \\
\text{(6)} \quad &amp; P_{3} \\
\text{(7)} \quad &amp; P_{4} \\
\text{(8)} \quad &amp; P_{5} \\
\text{(9)} \quad &amp; P_{17} \\
\text{(10)} \quad &amp; P_{9} \\
\text{(11)} \quad &amp; P_{20} \\
\text{(12)} \quad &amp; P_{21} \\
\text{(13)} \quad &amp; P_{24} \\
\text{(14)} \quad &amp; (P_{36} \land P_{37} \land P_{40}) \rightarrow P_{25} \\
\text{(15)} \quad &amp; (P_{20} \land P_{21}) \rightarrow P_{22} \\
\text{(16)} \quad &amp; (P_{1} \land P_{4} \land P_{5}) \rightarrow P_{27} \\
\text{(17)} \quad &amp; (P_{1} \land P_{4} \land P_{5} \land P_{22} \land P_{24}) \rightarrow P_{28} \\
\text{(18)} \quad &amp; P_{25} \rightarrow P_{26} \\
\text{(19)} \quad &amp; (P_{26} \land P_{1}) \rightarrow P_{29} \\
\text{(20)} \quad &amp; P_{38} \\
\text{(21)} \quad &amp; P_{62} \\
\text{(22)} \quad &amp; (P_{38} \land P_{62}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{26}
\end{aligned}

<a id="chrysostom_cannot_be_held_with_johns_case"></a>
**`chrysostom_cannot_be_held_with_johns_case`**

**Chrysostom's conclusion and John's strand cannot both be held.** John's strand
concludes that justification is by faith alone, and so that faith suffices.
Chrysostom concludes that it does not. No consistent reading holds every premise
of both.

A reader has to choose between Calvin's reading of John and
Chrysostom's conclusion as written out here. It does not claim which to
choose. Each rests on a step rated `disputed`.

Nor does it claim that the faith Chrysostom speaks of, right belief without a
right life, is the faith the Reformers say justifies. His conclusion is written
out here as "faith does not suffice". A reader who takes him to deny only what
James calls dead faith (see the section on James) need not choose.

```lean
theorem chrysostom_cannot_be_held_with_johns_case : ¬Satisfiable
    johnWithChrysostom
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="obedienceAsFruitSource"></a>
**`obedienceAsFruitSource`**

The step of the Reformed answer: from John 3:36 and Matthew 7:21, with the
obedience they require read as sanctification, to "faith suffices". Schreiner:
"the necessity of good works doesn't contradict sola fide" (p. 55). Calvin on
3:36: "He shows that enjoyment consists in faith." Rated `disputed`: Chrysostom
accepts both texts and denies that believing suffices, and Stanley holds works a
condition of final salvation.

```lean
def obedienceAsFruitSource : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work schreinerJustificationByWorks (Bib.Locus.pages 55 55),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work calvinJohn (Bib.Locus.adLoc Scripture.john3_36),
        Reference.work westminsterConfession (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "XVI.2"),
        Reference.work westminsterConfession (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "XIII.1")],
    tradition := Tradition.reformedProtestant,
    confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="sanctificationLine"></a>
**`sanctificationLine`** — Obedience as sanctification (the Reformed answer on John 3:36)

**The Reformed answer to Chrysostom, as a line.** John 3:36 and Matthew 7:21
are accepted as they stand. The obedience they require is read as
sanctification, the fruit of faith. So they add no condition to faith, and the
first half of John 3:36 holds as it is written: whoever believes has eternal
life.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{38} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{62} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; P_{39} \\
\text{(4)} \quad &amp; (P_{38} \land P_{62} \land P_{39}) \rightarrow P_{26} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; P_{26}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>
